message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with complex control logic, large caches, high clock speeds, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput rather than latency. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich, complex instruction set (x86, ARM, etc.) with support for many data types and advanced features. | Often a reduced instruction set tailored for SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations. |
| **Execution model** | Serial or lightly parallel; each core can execute a wide variety of instructions. | Highly parallel; each core executes the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously (SIMD). |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers, low latency access. | Smaller per‑core caches, larger shared memory, higher bandwidth but higher latency. |
| **Typical workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks, branching, I/O, single‑threaded performance. | Data‑parallel tasks like matrix multiplication, image processing, deep learning inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Power & heat** | Designed for low power per core, efficient at handling diverse tasks. | High throughput per watt for parallel workloads; can consume more power when fully utilized. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional programming languages (C/C++, Java, etc.) with standard threading libraries. | Requires specialized APIs (CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan) or high‑level frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) that expose parallelism. |

In short, a CPU excels at tasks that require quick decision making and low latency, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation on many data points at once. Modern systems often combine both: the CPU handles general control and orchestration, and the GPU accelerates compute‑heavy or graphics‑heavy parts.
